extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), patent examiners, and judges evaluating enablement and written-description issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and doctrinal criteria for determining whether a patent specification meets 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) (enablement) and related written-description considerations, with attention to claims that purport to cover broad genera (especially in biotechnology/antibody contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must describe the invention "in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make and use the [invention]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory command that secures the patent 'bargain' — a limited exclusivity in exchange for disclosure. Courts enforce the obligation to enable the invention as claimed. The opinion repeatedly cites the statutory text and historical practice; failure to meet this standard renders claims invalid. Examples and precedent citations (e.g., Bonito Boats, Morse) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable the full scope of the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent "claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the patent's specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims 'measure the invention.' The specification must enable the full scope of what the claims define — the broader the claim (e.g., an entire genus defined by function), the more that must be enabled. Illustrative precedents: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture. If the claimed class includes embodiments the specification does not teach, the claim may be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples may suffice only if a general quality running through the class is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may give one or a few examples and still enable a claimed class if it also discloses "some general quality ... running through" the class that gives it "a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incandescent Lamp shows that a few working examples can enable a broader genus when the inventor identifies a common characteristic that reliably guides others to make other embodiments. Absent such a disclosed common quality, examples alone are often insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable experimentation tolerated; undue experimentation is not
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a claimed invention; what is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Wood and Minerals Separation recognize that some adaptation/testing by a skilled artisan is acceptable. The key is whether the required experimentation is reasonable in light of the field, or instead amounts to undue experimentation that fails to constitute enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-descriptive claiming (describing inputs by function) can defeat enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing key inputs or class members only by their 'use or function' rather than their physical or chemical characteristics can leave artisans unable to make or use the invention without 'elaborate experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holland Furniture / Perkins Glue: where the specification described a 'starch ingredient' by function, claim was invalid for lack of enablement because practitioners would have to experiment extensively to find suitable materials. Guidance: when functionally defined elements are central, disclose structural/chemical/physical characteristics or other enabling criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial-and-error research assignments are not enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that merely instruct practitioners to 'try a large set' of candidates or to perform general trial-and-error screening (the opinion calls Amgen's "roadmap" and "conservative substitution" examples) do not enable a claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejects 'roadmap' approaches that amount to telling skilled artisans to engage in random or extensive trial-and-error (likened to a 'hunting license' or a combination-lock analogy). If the only disclosed way to reach claimed embodiments is open-ended trial-and-error, the specification fails enablement. Anti-pattern: instructions that amount to 'make lots of candidates and test them' without principled selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: The more one claims, the more one must enable
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more one claims, the more one must enable." Broad claims demanding monopoly over wide classes require correspondingly comprehensive enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle flows from matching claim scope to disclosure. Claim-drafting and specification drafting should anticipate that expanding claim breadth increases the disclosure burden. Practical rule: when seeking genus/functionally-defined claims, provide either many representative embodiments plus a disclosed unifying trait or sufficiently detailed methods to reliably make and use the genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement assessment focuses on quality of disclosure, not merely cumulative time/effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is not measured only by the cumulative time and effort it would take to make every embodiment within a claim; courts ask whether the disclosure gives adequate guidance beyond trial-and-error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit's consideration of how much effort is required is not dispositive; what matters is whether the specification provides adequate guidance to avoid undue experimentation. Even if making every embodiment would take long cumulative time, a specification can still be enabling if it provides reliable, instructive guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (distinct but related)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must include a written description of the invention and the manner and process of making and using it — enough to show the inventor possessed the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although distinct from enablement, written description often appears alongside enablement challenges. Jury findings and appellate reviews on written description (e.g., earlier trial verdicts in this case) inform validity analyses; adequacy requires particularity about claimed subject matter so the public can know what was invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art affects what disclosure suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the underlying science (predictable vs unpredictable technology) matters: in unpredictable fields (e.g., antibody sequence→structure/function mappings), broader claims require more detailed disclosure because substitutions can produce unpredictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In antibody/biotech contexts where a single amino-acid change can unpredictably alter function and where sequence-to-structure translation remains imperfectly understood, enabling a broad genus by generic methods (conservative substitution, roadmap) is less likely to succeed. Drafters should tailor disclosure to the predictability of the technology and provide structural detail, robust representative examples, or mechanistic principles where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be matched by particularity when necessary to avoid overbroad monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot claim more than it enables; claiming broadly without particularized disclosure 'would extend the monopoly beyond the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents warn against claiming entire 'kingdoms' of subject matter (telegraphic means, all fibrous materials, all starch glues that work) when the specification does not teach how to make and use them. Practical implication: limit claim scope or expand disclosure (characteristics, representative embodiments, enabling methods) to justify genus claims.
